claim: Assume J >= 5 for every tight pair in an S_4 tournament on 52 vertices, as proved in research/AGENT_TASKS/R1-C-n52-j-le-2.report.json and not re-proved here. Then every such pair has at least four dominators of in-degree greater than 25. Sections 5 and 9 of proof/N52_TIGHT_PAIRS.md reach that conclusion, but they do not follow as printed. The first gap is section 5, partition 6+3, on the degree shape (2, 2, 1): the pair counts are 18, 13 and 13, so the printed pair with 8 dominators does not occur. Section 9 omits the empty excess at J = 14 and several degree splits, and two printed budgets are wrong. The repaired case analysis below leaves no configuration with s <= 3. A tight pair with s >= 4 remains open, f(4) >= 52 is not proved, and Erdős problem 902 is not solved.
definitions: T is an S_4 tournament on N = 52 vertices: every 4-set has a dominator outside itself. Property S_4 is used only through the standing fact that every triple has at least 5 dominators. P is a tight pair, so R = D(P) has 11 vertices and T[R] is 5-regular. O = V \ (P union R) has 39 vertices. For y in O, q_y = |R intersect N^-(y)| >= 5 and the excess of y is q_y - 5. A vertex is heavy when q_y >= 6. For r in R, d^-(r) = 25 + j_r with j_r >= 0 and J = sum j_r. V_0 = {r in R : j_r = 0}, V_+ = R \ V_0, and s = |V_+|. The heavy excess is E = sum_y (q_y - 5) = 14 - J. For u in R, tau_u is the sum of (q_y - 5) over heavy y that beat u. lambda(5) = 0, lambda(6) = 4, lambda(7) = 7, lambda(8) = 9, lambda(9) = lambda(10) = 10. Ex(u) = 5 + 10 j_u - sum lambda(q_y), the sum running over y that beat u, and Ex(u) >= 0. For a pair of vertices in R, c is the number of vertices of R that beat both, E_both is the sum of (q_y - 5) over y that beat both, and D is the number of dominators of the pair. The triple excess of the pair is 4D - c - 45 - E_both. Lemma A is the input, rechecked in the R1-C report and not re-proved here: a vertex of excess 0 lies in every heavy in-neighbourhood, and every pair from it into the rest of R has 12 dominators. Consequently every heavy vertex beats only vertices of V_+. A heavy vertex of excess e beats exactly t = 6 - e vertices of R, so e lies in {6 - s, ..., 6}. Lemma J and the exclusion of J = 3 and J = 4 are the input J >= 5. They are not rebuilt.
argument:
Verdict. Under the input J >= 5, no tight pair has s <= 3. Equivalently, at least four vertices of D(P) have in-degree at least 26. The argument is the case analysis below. It uses Lemma A, the pair-sum, the triple-excess formula, c <= 4, and E = 14 - J. It does not reopen J = 3 or J = 4.

Tools, stated once. The winner of the edge between two vertices of R occupies one of the five in-neighbour slots of the loser, so c <= 4. The triple excess is therefore at least 4D - 49 - E_both, and it is at most Ex at each endpoint. In particular 4D - 45 >= 0, so every pair inside R has at least 12 dominators; a count of 11 or less makes the triple excess negative. For u in V_+, the pairs from u into V_0 number 11 - s and each has 12 dominators, so the pairs from u into the other positive vertices sum to 12(s - 1) + 5 j_u - tau_u. At s = 3 this says that the pair opposite vertex i has dominator count determined by the three linear equations. A 5-vertex contributes 0 to tau, to lambda, and to E_both, so only the heavy vertices in the excess partition appear.

J = 5, so E = 9. This is section 5.

s = 1. The excess of a heavy vertex lies in {5, 6}. The sums of such parts are 0, 5, 6, 10, 11, 12, and so on. None equals 9.

s = 2. The excesses lie in {4, 5, 6}, and the only partition of 9 is 5 + 4. The vertex of excess 4 beats both positive vertices. The vertex of excess 5 beats exactly one of them, and that one has tau = 9 while the other has tau = 4. The two expressions for the single pair agree only when the beaten vertex has j one larger than the other. With sum 5 this is the pair of degrees 3 and 2, the excess 5 lying on the degree 3. The pair has 12 + 15 - 9 = 18 dominators. E_both = 4, so the triple excess is at least 4*18 - 49 - 4 = 19. The degree 2 is beaten only by the excess-4 vertex, so its lambda sum is 10 and Ex = 5 + 20 - 10 = 15. Since 19 > 15, the case dies. The degree 3 has lambda sum 20 and Ex = 15 as well. The printed bound 19 is this number. The appeal to section 3 leaves E_both unstated; subtracting 4 is what produces 19 rather than 23.

s = 3. The excesses lie in {3, 4, 5, 6}. The partitions of 9 are 6 + 3, 5 + 4, and 3 + 3 + 3. Every composition of 5 into three positive parts is (3, 1, 1) or (2, 2, 1) up to order, so some part equals 1.

Partition 3 + 3 + 3. Three vertices of q = 8 beat all three positive vertices. Each contributes lambda = 9, so the lambda sum is 27 at every positive vertex. The part 1 has budget 15. This partition dies as printed. The part 2 has budget 25, and 27 exceeds that budget as well.

Partition 6 + 3. The excess-6 vertex beats nobody. The excess-3 vertex beats all three positive vertices, so every tau equals 3, every lambda sum is 9, and every pair has E_both = 3. The pair opposite a vertex of degree j has 23 - 5j dominators. On the shape (3, 1, 1) the pair opposite the part 3 has 8 dominators. That is the printed contradiction, and it applies only to this shape. On the shape (2, 2, 1) the counts are 13, 13, and 18, the last of them opposite the part 1. No pair has 8 dominators, so the printed sentence does not cover this shape. The pair of the two degree-2 vertices has triple excess at least 4*18 - 49 - 3 = 20, while each has Ex = 5 + 20 - 9 = 16. Since 20 > 16, the shape dies for that reason.

Partition 5 + 4. One vertex of q = 10 beats one positive vertex, and one vertex of q = 9 beats two. Write X and Y for the two beaten by the q = 9, and Z for the positive vertex it does not beat. Then E_both equals 4 on {X, Y} and equals 0 on the other two pairs. Up to swapping X and Y there are two placements of the q = 10.

If the q = 10 beats Z, then tau is 4, 4, 5 and every lambda sum is 10. The pair {X, Y} has 23 - 5 j_Z dominators. If j_Z >= 3, that count is at most 8. If j_Z = 1 and the other degrees are 3 and 1, the pair from Z to the remaining part 1 has (25 + 24 - 35)/2 = 7 dominators. If j_Z = 1 and the other degrees are 2 and 2, the pair {X, Y} has 18 dominators and triple excess at least 19, against Ex = 15 at either end. If j_Z = 2, the other degrees are 2 and 1; the pair from Z to the degree 2 has 17 dominators and triple excess at least 19, against Ex = 15 at both ends.

If the q = 10 beats X, then tau is 9, 4, 0 and the lambda sums are 20, 10, 0. The budget at X is negative when j_X = 1. The pair {Y, Z} has 27 - 5 j_X dominators, and j_X <= 3 because the three degrees sum to 5. If j_X = 3, then both remaining degrees are 1, the pair from X to Z has 17 dominators, and the triple excess is at least 19 against Ex = 15 at both ends. If j_X = 2 and the remaining degrees are 1 on Y and 2 on Z, the pair {X, Y} has 8 dominators. If j_X = 2 and the remaining degrees are 2 on Y and 1 on Z, the pair {Y, Z} has 17 dominators and triple excess at least 19 against Ex = 15 at both ends.

Every placement dies. The printed bullet names these three kinds of contradiction and does not give the placements. The placements are the missing text. Thus s >= 4 when J = 5.

J >= 6, so E = 14 - J <= 8. This is section 9. The same tools apply, and s <= 3 is the remaining obstacle.

s = 1. Excesses lie in {5, 6}, so for E <= 8 the possible sums are 0, 5, and 6. The ten pairs into V_0 have 12 dominators each, and the pair-sum reads 120 = 120 + 5J - tau, hence tau = 5J. An excess-6 vertex beats nobody, so the partition E = 6 has tau = 0, while J = 8 and 5J = 40. The partition E = 5 has tau = 5, while J = 9 and 5J = 45. The empty partition E = 0 has tau = 0, while J = 14 and 5J = 70. The printed text has the first two comparisons. It omits E = 0, and the sentence that no other value of E is a sum of parts in {5, 6} is false for the empty sum. The opening clause that every heavy vertex beats the unique positive vertex is false for an excess-6 vertex; the tau = 0 which the note then uses for E = 6 is the consistent value. All three partitions fail the equation. No sum of one or more parts from {5, 6} equals 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, or 8.

s = 2. Excesses lie in {4, 5, 6}. The sums at most 8 are 0, 4, 5, 6, and 8. The value 7 cannot be built, and neither can 1, 2, or 3. The two expressions for the single pair agree only for the degree patterns in the following list, and each of those patterns dies.

E = 8, partition 4 + 4. Both heavy vertices beat both positive vertices, so tau = 8 at each and the degrees are equal. Then J = 6 forces degrees 3, 3, the pair has 19 dominators, and E_both = 8. The triple excess is at least 19, while Ex = 5 + 30 - 20 = 15.

E = 6, one excess-6 vertex, which beats nobody. Then tau = 0 and the degrees are 4, 4. The pair has 32 dominators and E_both = 0, so the triple excess is at least 79, while Ex = 45.

E = 5, one excess-5 vertex, beating one endpoint. The tau difference is 5, so the degrees are 5 and 4 with the excess on the degree 5. The pair has 32 dominators and the triple excess is at least 79. Both endpoints have Ex = 45: the degree 5 loses 10 to lambda, and the degree 4 loses nothing.

E = 4, one excess-4 vertex, beating both. The degrees are 5, 5, the pair has 33 dominators, and E_both = 4. The triple excess is at least 79, while Ex = 45.

E = 0. There is no heavy vertex, the degrees are 7, 7, and the pair has 47 dominators. The triple excess is at least 139, while Ex = 75.

The four rows of the printed table match the four nonempty partitions, including the unique degree pattern in each row. The preamble that every row has budget at most 15 fits only the first row; the other three budgets are 45, as the cells state. The empty partition is the omission. The sentence that E <= 3 cannot be built is false for the empty sum and true for 1, 2, and 3.

s = 3. Excesses lie in {3, 4, 5, 6}. Three such parts sum to at least 9, so E <= 8 allows at most two heavy vertices. The possible data are E = 8 with parts 5 + 3 or 4 + 4, E = 7 with parts 4 + 3, E = 6 with parts 6 or 3 + 3, E = 5 with one part 5, E = 4 with one part 4, E = 3 with one part 3, and E = 0. Throughout, J = 14 - E.

E = 8, both excesses 4, beating the same pair. Both beat X and Y, and neither beats Z. Then tau is 8, 8, 0 and the lambda sums are 20, 20, 0, so E_both is 8 on {X, Y} and 0 on the pairs through Z. The pair {X, Y} has 19 - 5 j_Z dominators. Thus j_Z = 1 and that pair has 14 dominators; if j_Z >= 2 the count is at most 9. The remaining degrees sum to 5, and the pair from X to Z has 2 + 5 j_X dominators. The split (4, 1) puts 7 dominators on the pair from the part 1 to Z, and the part 1 has Ex = 5 + 10 - 20 = -5. The split (3, 2) puts 17 dominators on the pair from the part 3 to Z, with E_both = 0, so the triple excess is at least 19 against Ex(Z) = 15. The printed text asserts j_Z = 1 and then treats only the split in which one of the other degrees is 3. The split (4, 1) is the missing branch. Both branches die.

E = 8, the two excesses 4 beat different pairs. Two distinct 2-subsets of a 3-set meet in one vertex X. Then tau is 8, 4, 4, the lambda sums are 20, 10, 10, and E_both is 4 on each pair through X and 0 on the opposite pair. The budget forces j_X >= 2, and j_X <= 4. The opposite pair has 27 - 5 j_X dominators. If j_X = 4, that count is 7. The printed restriction j_X in {2, 3} omits this value; the budget 5 + 40 = 45 allows it, and the dominator count kills it. If j_X = 2, the opposite pair has 17 dominators and the remaining degrees sum to 4. The split (2, 2) gives triple excess at least 19 against Ex = 15 at either end. The split (3, 1) gives 8 dominators on the pair from X to the part 1. The printed sentence mentions only a degree-2 endpoint. If j_X = 3, the opposite pair has 12 dominators and the remaining degrees are 2 and 1. The pair from X to the degree 2 has 18 dominators and E_both = 4, so the triple excess is at least 19 against Ex = 15. This last branch is the printed one.

E = 8, excesses 5 and 3. The excess 3 beats all three positive vertices, and the excess 5 beats one vertex X. Then tau is 8, 3, 3, the lambda sums are 19, 9, 9, and every pair has E_both = 3. The budget forces j_X >= 2. The opposite pair has 28 - 5 j_X dominators. If j_X = 4, that count is 8. The printed text allows only j_X in {2, 3}. If j_X = 2, the opposite pair has 18 dominators and triple excess at least 20. An endpoint of degree j has Ex = 10j - 4, which is at least 20 only for j >= 3, and the two endpoints share degree sum 4. This is the printed argument, and it covers both (2, 2) and (3, 1). If j_X = 3, the remaining degrees are 2 and 1, the pair from X to the degree 2 has 18 dominators, and the triple excess is at least 20 against Ex = 16. This branch follows as printed.

E = 7, excesses 4 and 3. The excess 4 beats X and Y, and the excess 3 beats all three. Then tau is 7, 7, 3, the lambda sums are 19, 19, 9, E_both is 7 on {X, Y}, and E_both is 3 on the pairs through Z. The pair {X, Y} has 24 - 5 j_Z dominators, so j_Z >= 3 makes that count at most 9, and j_Z is 1 or 2. If j_Z = 1, the pair has 19 dominators and triple excess at least 20. An endpoint then needs degree at least 4, because Ex = 10j - 14 equals 16 at j = 3 and 26 at j = 4. The two endpoints would sum to at least 8, and the remaining degree sum is 6. This branch follows as printed. If j_Z = 2, the remaining degrees sum to 5 and the pair from X to Z has 3 + 5 j_X dominators. The split (4, 1) puts 8 dominators on the pair from the part 1 to Z, and that part has Ex = -4. The split (3, 2) puts 18 dominators on the pair from the part 3 to Z, with triple excess at least 20 against Ex(Z) = 16. The printed text says that one endpoint has degree 3, which is the second split only.

E = 6, one vertex of excess 6. It beats nobody, so every tau, lambda sum, and E_both is 0, and J = 8. The pair opposite a vertex of degree j has 32 - 5j dominators. A part of 5 or more leaves at most 7 dominators, so every composition of 8 that survives this test is (4, 3, 1), (4, 2, 2), or (3, 3, 2), up to order. Opposite the part 1 the pair has 27 dominators and triple excess at least 59, while each endpoint has degree at most 4 and Ex at most 45. Opposite a part 2 in (4, 2, 2), the other endpoint of that pair has degree 2 and Ex = 25, against triple excess at least 39. Opposite the part 2 in (3, 3, 2), both endpoints have Ex = 35, against the same 39. This bullet follows as printed.

E = 6, two vertices of excess 3. Both beat all three positive vertices, so every lambda sum is 18, every tau is 6, and every E_both is 6. The budget forces every degree to be at least 2. The pair opposite a vertex of degree j has 29 - 5j dominators, so a part 4 leaves 9 dominators. The only remaining composition of 8 is (3, 3, 2). Opposite the part 2 the pair has 19 dominators and triple excess at least 21, while each endpoint has Ex = 5 + 30 - 18 = 17. This bullet follows as printed.

E = 5, one vertex of excess 5, beating X. Then tau_X = 5, the other two tau values are 0, E_both = 0 on every pair, and J = 9. The pair opposite X has 37 - 5 j_X dominators. The pair opposite either of the other vertices, of degree j, has 32 - 5j dominators, so each of those degrees is at most 4, and j_X itself is at most 5. The printed sentence that no degree exceeds 5 is true; the two vertices other than X are held to 4.

If j_X = 1, the only remaining composition with both other degrees at most 4 is (4, 4). The opposite pair has 32 dominators and triple excess at least 79, while each endpoint has Ex = 45. The printed comparison, triple excess at least 39 against Ex at most 35, fits neither number. This composition does not follow as printed, and 79 > 45 kills it.

If j_X = 2, the opposite pair has 27 dominators and triple excess at least 59. The other degrees sum to 7 and are at most 4, so they are 4 and 3. The smaller has Ex = 35. Already the printed lower bound 39 exceeds 35, and the sharp count 59 exceeds the larger budget 45 as well.

If j_X = 3, the opposite pair has 22 dominators and triple excess at least 39. The other degrees sum to 6, so the smaller is at most 3 and has Ex at most 35. This is the printed comparison, and it applies.

If j_X = 4, the other degrees sum to 5 and are at most 4, so the split is (3, 2) or (4, 1), not only (2, 3). On (3, 2) the pair from X to the degree 3 has 22 dominators and triple excess at least 39, against Ex = 35 at X and at the degree 3. That subcase follows as printed. On (4, 1) the pair from X to the degree 4 has 27 dominators and triple excess at least 59, against Ex(X) = 35 and Ex = 45 at the degree 4. The printed sentence does not contain this split.

If j_X = 5, the other degrees sum to 4. On (3, 1) the pair from X to the part 1 has 17 dominators and triple excess at least 19, against Ex = 15. On (2, 2) each pair from X has 22 dominators and triple excess at least 39, against Ex = 25. This is the printed alternative, and it covers both splits.

E = 4, one vertex of excess 4, beating X and Y and not Z. Then tau is 4, 4, 0, the lambda sums are 10, 10, 0, E_both is 4 on {X, Y}, and J = 10. A missed vertex of degree j has Ex = 10j - 5. The pair {X, Y} has 33 - 5 j_Z dominators.

If j_Z >= 5, that count is at most 8. This sentence follows as printed.

If j_Z = 1, the pair has 28 dominators and triple excess at least 59, so each missed vertex needs degree at least 7. The remaining degree sum is 9, and 7 + 7 = 14 > 9. The printed necessary condition that each degree is at least 5 would already give 5 + 5 = 10 > 9, but the printed remainder is described as at most 8. The remainder on this line is 9. The sharp bound is the one used here.

If j_Z = 2, the pair has 23 dominators and triple excess at least 39, so each missed vertex needs degree at least 5. The remaining sum is 8. This line follows as printed.

If j_Z = 3, the pair {X, Y} has 18 dominators and some missed degree is at least 4. The pair from a missed vertex of degree j to Z has 2 + 5j dominators. For j = 4 the count is 22 and the triple excess is at least 39, against Ex = 35 at that vertex. The printed Ex(Z) = 45 is wrong: j_Z = 3 and the lambda sum at Z is 0, so Ex(Z) = 35. The budget 35 at the degree-4 end is enough for this split, since 39 > 35. For j = 5 the count is 27 and the triple excess is at least 59, against Ex = 45 at the degree 5 and Ex(Z) = 35. For j = 6 the count is 32 and the triple excess is at least 79, against Ex = 55; the pair from Z to the remaining part 1 also has 7 dominators. The printed text stops at degree 4.

If j_Z = 4, the splits of the remaining 6 are (3, 3), (4, 2), and (5, 1). The pair from Z to the larger missed vertex has 22, 27, or 32 dominators, hence triple excess at least 39, 59, or 79. The budgets at those missed vertices are 25, 35, and 45. This line follows as printed.

E = 3, one vertex of excess 3, beating all three. Every tau is 3, every lambda sum is 9, every E_both is 3, and J = 11. The pair opposite a vertex of degree j has 38 - 5j dominators. Some degree is at most 3, because three degrees at least 4 would sum to at least 12. Opposite a part 1, 2, or 3 the dominator counts are 33, 28, and 23, and the triple excesses are at least 80, 60, and 40. The endpoints then need degrees at least 9, 7, and 5, with required sums 18, 14, and 10 against remaining sums 10, 9, and 8. Whichever part is the smallest, the corresponding line applies. This bullet follows as printed.

E = 0 at s = 3. There is no heavy vertex, every tau and E_both is 0, and J = 14. The pair opposite a vertex of degree j has 47 - 5j dominators. Some degree is at most 4. Opposite a part 4 the triple excess is at least 59, so both endpoints need degree at least 6 and the remaining sum 10 is too small. Opposite a part 3, 2, or 1 the triple excess is at least 79, 99, or 119, forcing endpoint degrees at least 8, 10, or 12, against remaining sums 11, 12, and 13. The printed closing sentence says that E <= 2 is not a sum of integers at least 3. That sentence is false for the empty sum and true for E = 1 and E = 2, neither of which can be built from parts at least 3.

Every configuration with J >= 5 and s <= 3 has been excluded. Therefore s >= 4. At J = 5 the inequality s <= J then forces s in {4, 5}; that refinement is not required for the count of four. Nothing here excludes a tight pair whose positive dominators number four or more. The order of f(4) is unchanged, and Erdős problem 902 is not solved.

labeled_enumeration.description: Every nondecreasing excess list with parts in {6 - s, ..., 6}, every assignment of miss-sets of size 6 - e inside V_+, and every ordered positive degree vector of sum J, for J from 5 through 14 and s from 1 through 3. A configuration survives only if every Ex is nonnegative, the pair-sum produces integer dominator counts of at least 12, and each positive pair admits an integer c in {0, 1, 2, 3, 4} whose triple excess lies between 0 and the smaller endpoint budget.

weaknesses: The status conditional belongs to the dependence on J >= 5. That bound is the R1-C report, written by the same agent role, and it is unreviewed. This report does not re-prove it, and it does not re-prove Lemma A. Every pair into V_0 is given 12 dominators by Lemma A; if that lemma failed, the pair-sum reduction used here would fail with it. The repaired case analysis is the argument for s >= 4 given those inputs. The printed section 5 does not establish the shape (2, 2, 1) of partition 6+3, and it does not write the placements of partition 5+4. The printed section 9 does not treat J = 14, and the splits and budgets named in the evidence do not follow as written. The introduction of proof/swarm/r1_AUDIT-52-B.md asserts Lemma C and sketches a uniform counting invariant, but the file stops during its section 3, before any such proof. That introduction is not evidence. The labeled enumeration is a check that the same inequalities admit no survivor; it is not a search of tournaments, and it uses the same identities as the case analysis, so it does not insure those identities. A tight pair with four or more positive dominators remains possible. f(4) >= 52 is not proved, and Erdős problem 902 is not solved.
next_step: Have a second reader check the repaired placements in section 5, partition 5+4, and the section 9 composition E = 5, j_X = 1, degrees (4, 4), against the pair-sum. The open half of Lemma C is s >= 4: the excess can still sit on four or more dominators, and that regime is what a surviving tight pair at order 52 would have to satisfy.
